Trigger: Finalizing a broad “Are there any abnormalities?” answer when one tool says “No” for a limited abnormality checklist but another tool reports positive findings.

Observable verification action: Enumerate every abnormal finding reported across tool observations and compare each negative answer with its exact scope. If the question asks broadly about any abnormality and any observation reports one—such as an atherosclerotic aorta, sternal suture fracture, or post-sternotomy change—answer Yes and cite that observed finding. Do not let a narrow “No” for consolidation/effusion/pneumothorax/cardiomegaly overrule a broader positive report. If choices are present, also map the supported answer text back to the displayed option and verify the letter and text agree.

Trigger: Finalizing a comparative organ-abnormality answer such as “Which organ is abnormal, heart or lung?” when the terminal rationale cites a grounded imaging report.

Observable verification action: Locate the raw grounded-report statement for each candidate organ. Choose the organ only if its statement contains an explicit abnormal finding (for example, “mildly prominent cardiac silhouette” or “cardiomegaly”) and the other organ’s statement is explicitly negative or normal (for example, “lungs are free of infiltrates and masses”). Do not infer a heart abnormality from a normal-lung statement alone. If the raw tool observation containing the cited report phrase is absent from the transcript, do not treat the correct final grade as proof of the evidence procedure; retrieve or rerun the grounded report/verify step first. If options are displayed, map the supported organ text back to the displayed choice and confirm the letter and text agree. In this case no options were present, so the relevant check is evidence attribution: the answer “heart” is supported only if the grounded report actually names the cardiac abnormality while clearing the lungs.

Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no “Is the lung healthy?” answer and the draft rationale cites specific imaging findings—such as pleural effusions or atelectasis—but the current trajectory has no raw image/report/tool observation explicitly documenting those findings for the lung.

Observable verification action: Re-read the available raw tool observations and confirm that at least one explicitly names the same organ/attribute and supports each cited abnormality. If such an observation is present, use it and confirm the final yes/no polarity matches it. If it is absent, do not present the finding as observed evidence; revise the rationale to a documented finding or retrieve/rerun the necessary observation before finalizing. If contradictory observations exist, resolve them before choosing. In this case, “No” matched the released reference, but the rationale cited bilateral pleural effusions and right lung base atelectasis while the observations were empty, so the correct grade alone does not verify the evidence path. If options were displayed, map the supported answer text back to the listed choice and check that its letter and text agree.
